text: FDA cites 400 mg/day as the amount not generally associated with negative effects for most adults.
quote: For most adults, the FDA has cited 400 milligrams* a day — that's about two to three 12-fluid-ounce cups of coffee — as an amount not generally associated with negative effects.

text: FDA advises pregnant, trying-to-conceive, or breastfeeding people to talk to their provider about limiting caffeine.
quote: if you’re pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, we recommend talking to your health care provider about whether you need to limit caffeine consumption.

text: FDA estimates toxic effects such as seizures can occur with rapid consumption of about 1,200 mg of caffeine.
quote: The FDA estimates toxic effects, like seizures, can be observed with rapid consumption of around 1,200 milligrams of caffeine, or less than 1/2 teaspoon of pure caffeine.

text: A 2017 systematic review (IAFNS) confirmed the safety of the 400 mg/day level for most adults, meeting NAS/IOM systematic-review standards.
quote: A 2017 systematic review of health outcomes associated with caffeine intake by the Institute for the Advancement of Food and Nutrition Sciences confirmed the safety of the 400 milligrams a day level for most adults.

text: ACOG concludes moderate caffeine intake (<200 mg/day) does not appear to be a major contributor to miscarriage or preterm birth.
quote: Moderate caffeine consumption (less than 200 mg per day) does not appear to be a major contributing factor in miscarriage or preterm birth.

text: One prospective cohort study (Weng et al.) found an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.23 for miscarriage at caffeine intake ≥200 mg/day.
quote: the investigators found an increased risk of miscarriage with higher levels of caffeine consumption, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.23 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34–3.69) for intake of 200 mg per day or more.

text: Another prospective study (Savitz et al.) found caffeine consumption at any level was unrelated to miscarriage risk, contradicting Weng et al.
quote: levels of caffeine consumption at all three time points and at all levels of consumption were unrelated to the risk of miscarriage.

text: A study of low-risk pregnancies found intrauterine growth restriction odds ratios rose with caffeine intake, peaking at 200–299 mg/day (OR 1.5).
quote: consumption of 100–199 mg per day (OR, 1.2; 95% CI, 0.9–1.6), 200–299 mg per day (OR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.1–2.1), and more than 300 mg per day (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.0–2.0).

text: A meta-analysis of 8 articles/14 studies found caffeine intake overall increased anxiety risk (SMD 0.94) in healthy individuals without psychiatric disorders.
quote: the results of the meta-analysis showed that caffeine intake increased the risk of anxiety [SMD = 0.94, 95% Cl = (0.28, 1.60), p< 0.05]

text: Subgroup analysis found high-dose caffeine (≥400 mg) produced a much larger anxiety increase than low-dose (<400 mg) caffeine.
quote: the high-dose caffeine (≥400 mg) group had a significantly higher increased risk of anxiety than the low-dose caffeine (<400 mg) group [SMD = 2.86, 95% Cl = (2.50, 3.22), p< 0.05]

text: Even low-dose (<400 mg) caffeine intake was associated with a statistically significant, moderate increase in anxiety risk (SMD 0.61), not zero effect.
quote: low-dose caffeine intake moderately increased the risk of anxiety [SMD = 0.61, 95%Cl = (0.42, 0.79), p< 0.05]

text: The authors recommend caffeine intake in healthy populations not exceed 400 mg/day, aligning with FDA guidance.
quote: we recommend that caffeine intake in healthy populations does not exceed 400 mg per day.

text: A meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials found unfiltered (but not filtered) coffee raises total and LDL cholesterol.
quote: Consumption of unfiltered, but not filtered, coffee increases serum levels of total and LDL cholesterol.

text: Trials of filtered coffee showed very little increase in serum cholesterol compared with boiled/unfiltered coffee.
quote: Trials using filtered coffee demonstrated very little increase in serum cholesterol.

text: Cholesterol increases from coffee were greater in patients with pre-existing hyperlipidemia and in trials of caffeinated or boiled coffee.
quote: Increases in serum lipids were greater in studies of patients with hyperlipidemia and in trials of caffeinated or boiled coffee.

text: EFSA's 2015 scientific opinion concluded single caffeine doses up to 200 mg and daily intake up to 400 mg do not raise safety concerns for healthy adults.
quote: In healthy adults and the elderly, single doses of caffeine of up to 200 mg (approximately 2 ½ espressos or 4 cups of tea) do not raise any safety concerns.

text: EFSA concluded regular caffeine intake up to 200 mg/day is safe for the unborn child or breastfed infant, matching the ACOG pregnancy threshold.
quote: For pregnant and breastfeeding women, EFSA concludes that regular caffeine consumption of up to 200 mg per day are safe for the unborn child or breastfed infant.

text: EFSA's opinion notes caffeine can affect sleep and sleep patterns at doses around 100 mg in certain individuals, especially near bedtime.
quote: It has also been shown to affect sleep and sleep patterns, at doses of around 100 mg in certain individuals, particularly when consumed close to bedtime.
